summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers the early life, family and political career of John, King of England, before his accession to the throne. It describes his marriages and the fates of his legitimate and illegitimate children, his involvement in the war with Philip II and his role in Ireland, and his position under his brother Richard I during the Third Crusade. It also traces the succession disputes of Henry II's sons, the rebellion of 1173 to 1174, and the 1191 clash between John and Longchamp in England.
one_line: Wikipedia article excerpt on the early life, family, Irish lordship and political rivalries of John, King of England, before he became king.
key_facts: John's first wife, Isabel, Countess of Gloucester, was released from imprisonment in 1214 and died in 1217.
John had five legitimate children, all by his second wife Isabella of Angoulême.
Henry III, John's eldest legitimate son, ruled as king for the majority of the 13th century.
Joan, John's legitimate daughter, married Alexander II of Scotland to become his queen consort.
John had nine illegitimate sons and three illegitimate daughters by various mistresses, with Joan marrying Prince Llywelyn the Great of Wales.
At the battle of Mirebeau, John's forces caught Arthur by surprise and captured the entire rebel leadership.
In 1210 John crossed into Ireland with a large army to crush a rebellion by the Anglo-Norman lords.
When Richard became king in September 1189, he had already declared his intention of joining the Third Crusade.
Richard left political authority in England jointly to Bishop Hugh de Puiset and William Mandeville, and made William Longchamp, the Bishop of Ely, his chancellor.
Richard named the four-year-old Arthur of Brittany as the heir to the throne, while John promised not to visit England for three years.
John was jokingly nicknamed "Lackland" by his father because he seemed unlikely to inherit substantial lands.
Henry II transferred the castles of Chinon, Loudun and Mirebeau into John's name when John was about five years old, as part of a betrothal to Alais of Savoy.
Alais died before marrying John, leaving the prince once again without an inheritance.
The rebellion of 1173 to 1174 saw John's elder brothers, backed by Eleanor, revolt against Henry II; Eleanor was the only one imprisoned for her role.
The war between Henry the Young King and Richard in 1183 ended with Henry the Young King dying from dysentery at the end of the campaign.
The war between John and Richard's forces ended in stalemate and a family reconciliation in England at the end of 1184.
By October 1191 Longchamp was isolated in the Tower of London, with John in control of the city of London.
Walter of Coutances, Archbishop of Rouen, returned to England after Richard sent him to restore order, and news of Richard's marriage in Cyprus undermined John's position.
